issues.legal_issue: A state legislature may acquire property belonging to an undertaking in an industry declared for central control when the acquisition is within its independent acquisition power and does not intrude on the field occupied by central regulation.
material_facts: The challenged state law transferred and vested scheduled sugar undertakings in a state corporation.
The central legislation governed the development and regulation of declared industries, including sugar, but did not generally govern ownership of their undertakings.
After the transfer, the undertakings remained subject to central control under the central legislation.
The state law’s provisions, viewed as a whole, dealt with acquisition of the undertakings.
issues.conclusion: The state legislature was competent to enact the acquisition law, and it did not conflict with or intrude upon the field occupied by the central legislation.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 246 and Entries 24 of List II, 52 of List I, and 42 of List III, acquisition of property is an independent legislative power under Entry 42, exercisable by both Parliament and the States. A declaration under Entry 52 removes state legislative power under Entry 24 only to the extent of the control occupied by the legislation enacted pursuant to the declaration. The law’s pith and substance determines its character, and incidental effects on another field do not invalidate it. The Court relied on Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, Rajamundry Electric Supply Corporation Ltd. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh, State of West Bengal v. Union of India, Kannan Devan Hills Produce Company Ltd. v. State of Kerala, Baijnath Kedia v. State of Bihar, and State of Haryana v. Chanan Mal.

rule.if: challenge_to_state_acquisition_law and law_acquires_industrial_property and acquisition_power_is_separate and central_law_regulates_industry_without_acquiring_property

predicates.challenge_to_state_acquisition_law: A party challenges the legislative competence of a state law that acquires an industrial undertaking.
predicates.law_acquires_industrial_property: The law’s provisions, in substance, transfer ownership of property belonging to an industrial undertaking.
predicates.acquisition_power_is_separate: The acquisition is an exercise of legislative power specifically concerning acquisition of property, rather than merely an incident of power over another subject.
predicates.central_law_regulates_industry_without_a: The central law regulates the industry but does not itself acquire the undertaking’s property.

issues.definition: When a state acquisition law acquires industrial property under a separate acquisition power and the central law regulates the industry without acquiring that property, the state law is within legislative competence.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory prohibition on a state executive authority taking over an industrial undertaking’s management does not bar management from passing to an acquiring authority as a consequence of a valid legislative acquisition.
material_facts: The central legislation prohibited a state government or local authority from taking over an industrial undertaking’s management or control under executive authority.
The challenged state law was enacted to acquire the scheduled undertakings, not to take over their management or control by executive action.
Any transfer of management or control followed from the vesting of the undertakings in the acquiring corporation.
issues.conclusion: The consequential transfer of management or control following the acquisition did not violate the statutory prohibition.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951, inhibits executive action by a state government or local authority to take over an undertaking’s management or control. It does not prevent a transfer of management or control that follows as an incident of a valid legislative acquisition under a legislative power other than the state’s industry power.

rule.if: challenge_to_acquisition_law and law_acquires_industrial_undertaking and no_executive_management_takeover and management_transfer_follows_acquisition

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_law: A party challenges a law that acquires an industrial undertaking.
predicates.law_acquires_industrial_undertaking: The law’s substance is the acquisition and transfer of ownership of the undertaking.
predicates.no_executive_management_takeover: The state authority does not independently take over management or control through executive action.
predicates.management_transfer_follows_acquisition: Management or control passes to the acquiring authority as a consequence of the acquisition.

issues.definition: When a law acquires an industrial undertaking without an independent executive takeover, a resulting transfer of its management is not barred.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired property satisfies the constitutional requirement when it is determined by relevant principles and is not shown to be illusory, even if its adequacy is challenged.
material_facts: The acquisition law set compensation for the scheduled undertakings in specified amounts.
The compensation calculation applied a principle accepted by the Court as relevant to valuing used machinery.
The undertakings had substantial carried-forward losses, had failed to pay cane growers and labour, and remained in serious difficulty despite earlier management intervention.
The appellants challenged the compensation as inadequate and illusory.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the compensation under Article 31(2), as it then stood, failed; the adequacy of compensation calculated using the relevant principle was not open to judicial review.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as it stood at the relevant time, required compensation for compulsory acquisition. A specified principle is open to challenge if it is irrelevant to determining value or produces illusory compensation, but the Court will not review adequacy where a relevant, recognized principle is applied. The Court relied on Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector of Land Acquisition, Union of India v. Metal Corporation of India, State of Gujarat v. Shantilal Mangaldas, and His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalavaru v. State of Kerala.

predicates.challenge_to_compensation_in_acquisition: A party challenges the compensation provided in a compulsory-acquisition case.
predicates.compensation_principle_is_relevant: The compensation is determined using a principle relevant to valuing the property acquired.
predicates.compensation_is_not_shown_illusory: The challenger does not establish that applying the principle makes the compensation illusory.

issues.definition: In an acquisition case, a compensation challenge fails when the valuation principle is relevant and the compensation is not shown to be illusory.

issues.legal_issue: Selecting undertakings for acquisition does not violate equality when the selected undertakings form a group distinguished by serious financial and payment defaults that rationally relate to the acquisition’s public purpose.
material_facts: The law acquired twelve scheduled sugar undertakings, while other sugar undertakings were not acquired.
The government reviewed the condition of the undertakings and considered persistent defaults in payments to cane growers, labour, and others.
The record identified the selected undertakings as being in a desperate or intolerable condition.
The acquisition sought to revive the undertakings and improve the local economy, including by prioritizing payments to cane growers and labour.
issues.conclusion: The classification of the selected undertakings had an intelligible differentia rationally connected to the law’s object, and the equality challenge failed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits differential treatment where the classification rests on an intelligible differentia and that differentia has a rational relationship to the object sought to be achieved. The Court applied this principle to the government’s classification of undertakings in an intolerable economic condition for acquisition.

predicates.equality_challenge_to_selective_acquisit: A party alleges unequal treatment because some undertakings were selected for acquisition while others were not.
predicates.government_assesses_undertaking_conditio: The government reviews and compares the economic and payment conditions of the undertakings.
predicates.selected_undertakings_have_severe_defaul: The selected undertakings have serious financial difficulties or persistent defaults affecting those owed payment.
predicates.classification_relates_to_public_objecti: Selecting the distressed undertakings is rationally connected to the stated objective of addressing those conditions and their public consequences.

issues.definition: Selective acquisition does not violate equality when the government assesses undertaking conditions, selects those with severe defaults, and the selection is rationally connected to the public objective.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that separate agricultural land was acquired without compensation is not established without evidence that the land was in fact acquired as part of the undertaking.
material_facts: An appellant asserted that agricultural land belonging to the undertaking’s owner had been taken without compensation.
The record and pleadings did not establish whether agricultural land outside the structures of the undertaking had been acquired or taken over.
The Court noted that open land between structures could be part and parcel of the undertaking.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the claim because the record did not specifically establish that separate agricultural land had been acquired or taken over.
issues.legal_principle: A claim of uncompensated acquisition of separate land requires a factual showing that the land was acquired or taken over as part of the acquisition; the Court would not infer that fact from an unclear record.

predicates.uncompensated_land_claim_in_acquisition_: A party claims that land was acquired without compensation in an acquisition case.
predicates.separate_land_is_alleged: The party alleges that land separate from the acquired undertaking’s structures was taken.
predicates.record_does_not_establish_separate_land_: The evidence does not specifically establish that the separate land was acquired or taken over.

issues.definition: A claim of uncompensated land acquisition is not established when separate land is alleged but the record does not show that it was taken.

issues.legal_issue: Goodwill need not be separately valued as part of compensation for an acquired undertaking when the acquired property does not include the company, partnership, or proprietorship that owns it.
material_facts: The acquisition law acquired the scheduled undertakings, not the companies, partnerships, or proprietorships that owned them.
The appellants sought to include goodwill in the valuation of the undertakings.
The undertakings were described as sick units with substantial carried-forward losses and payment defaults.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the goodwill claim because the owners, to which goodwill could belong, were not acquired under the law.
issues.legal_principle: Goodwill may belong to a company, partnership, or proprietor, but not as a separately valued component of a manufacturing undertaking in the circumstances considered. Where the acquisition takes the undertaking but not its owner, the owner’s goodwill is not part of the acquired property to be valued.

predicates.goodwill_claim_in_acquisition_case: A party claims that goodwill must be included in compensation in an acquisition case.
predicates.undertaking_is_acquired: The acquired property is an industrial or manufacturing undertaking.
predicates.owning_entity_is_not_acquired: The company, partnership, or proprietor that owns the undertaking is not itself acquired.

issues.definition: When an undertaking is acquired but its owning entity is not, the owning entity’s goodwill is not a component of compensation for the undertaking.
